title: Operate and maintain specific irrigation systems

lessons.title: Pre-start inspection of your system
lessons.html:
Know your system

This unit is about operating one specific system well. Common systems on South African farms are:

  • Drip: drippers along lines give water at each plant. Used in orchards, vineyards, vegetables and tunnels.
  • Micro-sprinklers: small sprinklers under trees in citrus and subtropical orchards.
  • Sprinkler (dragline or permanent): sprinklers on risers in vegetables, pastures and sugar cane.
  • Centre pivot: a long pipe on towers that turns around a centre point over maize, wheat, lucerne or potatoes.

Pre-start inspection checklist

Do this before every start. A five-minute check can prevent a day of damage.

  1. Water source: enough water in the dam, canal or reservoir; suction strainer clear of weeds and debris.
  2. Pump station: no leaks, guards on couplings, area clear. Only trained people open electrical panels.
  3. Filters: clean. Check pressure gauges before and after the filter; a big difference means it is dirty.
  4. Fertigation unit (if used): set as instructed, connected correctly, back-flow valve in place.
  5. Valves: correct valves open for the block to irrigate, others closed.
  6. Lines: no visible cuts, kinks or loose end plugs.
  7. Centre pivot: wheel tracks clear, tyres inflated, no tools, animals, vehicles or people in the path, towers aligned, end gun working.

Write down what you checked and any faults. Report faults before starting if they are serious.

Safety

  • Pivots and pump stations use high-voltage electricity. Never open control boxes unless trained and authorised. Report damaged cables at once.
  • Never climb on a pivot or stand in front of moving towers.
  • Keep clear of pump couplings and belts.
  • Fertigation chemicals and acids need PPE; follow the label and your supervisor.

lessons.title: Start-up, irrigating and shut-down
lessons.html:
Start-up procedure

  1. Confirm the block, irrigation time or depth from the schedule your supervisor gives you.
  2. Prime the pump if needed, as you were shown.
  3. Start the pump with the delivery valve partly closed, then open it slowly to bring pressure up gradually. This prevents water hammer.
  4. Check pressure at the pump and at the block. Compare with the normal pressure on the farm's record sheet.
  5. For a pivot: set direction, speed (percentage timer) and end gun as instructed, then start. Watch the first towers move properly.
  6. Write down the start time and pressure readings, and the meter reading if there is a water meter.

Irrigating according to guidelines

The farm's irrigation schedule says how much water each block needs, based on crop, growth stage, soil and weather. Your job is to apply it accurately.

  • Walk or drive the block during irrigation. Look for burst pipes, blocked emitters, broken sprinklers and dry or wet spots.
  • Watch for run-off and puddles. Report them; the system may be running too long or at the wrong pressure.
  • Avoid sprinkler irrigation in strong wind if your supervisor has said so; water blows away.
  • During fertigation, run clean water before and after the fertiliser, as instructed, so lines are flushed.
  • Check soil moisture with the method your farm uses: probe, tensiometer reading or digging.

Shut-down procedure

  1. Close valves slowly or stop the pump as the procedure says.
  2. For a pivot, stop it in the position the supervisor wants and make sure it is safe.
  3. Record the stop time, final meter reading and any faults.
  4. Drain lines in frost areas if the farm requires it.

Report straight away if the system will not reach normal pressure, a pivot stops with a fault, or the pump makes strange noises.

lessons.title: Care of equipment and tools
lessons.html:
Routine maintenance

Good maintenance keeps water even across the land and saves money.

Drip and micro systems

  • Clean screen and disc filters regularly; backflush sand filters as shown.
  • Flush drip lines by opening the ends until clean water runs.
  • Replace blocked or broken drippers and micro-sprinklers with the same type and flow rate. A different flow rate gives some plants more water than others.
  • Repair rat, mole or hoe damage with joiners.
  • Some farms treat lines with acid or chlorine to clear blockages. Only trained workers do this, with full PPE.

Sprinklers

  • Check nozzles for wear and blockage; replace worn nozzles with the correct size.
  • Keep risers upright and sprinklers turning freely.
  • Move draglines carefully so pipes and fittings do not break.

Centre pivots

  • Check tyre pressures and wheel gearbox oil as the schedule says.
  • Check sprinkler packages and drops for damage or blockage.
  • Fill or level deep wheel tracks so towers do not get stuck.
  • Report alignment faults and electrical faults to a qualified technician.

Pumps

  • Keep the pump house clean and dry.
  • Report leaks, overheating, vibration or noise.
  • Grease as shown, only when the pump is switched off and locked out.

Caring for tools

Clean spades, cutters, spanners and punches after use. Store spare fittings sorted by size. Return tools and report broken ones. Keep a small repair kit with joiners and plugs ready.

Records

Record dates, times, pressures, meter readings, faults and repairs. Records help the farm manage water use and show it is using water responsibly under its water use authorisation.

Key points

  • Do a pre-start inspection every time.
  • Start and stop slowly to avoid water hammer.
  • Apply the schedule accurately and watch for run-off.
  • Replace emitters with the same type and flow rate.
  • Never open electrical panels unless trained; never climb a pivot.
